latin: Intuitus diuinae cognitionis ad creaturas tanquam obiecta primaria uel secundaria formaliter non terminatur, ut dicit communis schola theologorum, sed se tantum et nihil aliud a se intuens primarie nec secundarie, unitiue et eminenter, et plus quam aequipollenter, omnia cognoscit. Correlarium: Non est aliqua multitudo intellectorum in deo, nec creature ut intellecte ponunt in numerum cum diuina essentia ut intellecta, sed est penitus unum simplicissimum intellectum.
latin_note: 1486 punctuates 'tantum.& nihil' and reads 'primariae nec secundariae'; 1487 reads 'primarie nec secundane'.
translation: The gaze of divine cognition does not terminate formally on creatures as primary or secondary objects, as the common school of theologians holds; rather, beholding only itself and nothing besides — neither as a primary nor a secondary object — it knows all things in a unitive, elevated way that exceeds mere equivalence to the task. Corollary: there is no plurality of things understood in God, nor do creatures, as understood, add up to a number alongside the divine essence as understood; at bottom there is but one utterly simple understanding.
